procedural_history.originating_court: District Judge, Kanpur; application under section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 15.04.2019 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in CRMWP Nos.31343 and 31370 of 2018.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court allowed the petitions on the finding that no offence under various sections mentioned in the FIR were made out as the same on its face value did not satisfy the requirements.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court because the High Court quashed the FIR lodged by the appellant against respondents u/ss.457, 380 and 506, IPC. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals and set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court. The matter was ordered to proceed with respect to the FIR in question in accordance with law.

directions: The impugned judgment of the High Court is set aside.
Law to take its own course.
The matter to proceed with respect to the FIR in question in accordance with law.

It is however made clear that any observations made in this order are only for the purposes of deciding the issue raised and the same may not inﬂuence the investigation or the trial which shall proceed independently and be decided on the evidence adduced.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the FIR lodged by the appellant against the respondents under sections 457, 380 and 506 of the IPC.

facts: The appellant filed a First Information Report (FIR) against the respondents for offenses under sections 457 (house-breaking), 380 (theft), and 506 (criminal intimidation) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The FIR alleged that the respondents broke open the locks of a shop, removed assets and belongings, and when the appellant questioned respondent No. 1, he was threatened with his life.
The High Court reviewed the FIR and quashed it, finding that on its face, the ingredients for the alleged offenses were not satisfied.
law: Section 506 of the IPC pertains to the offense of criminal intimidation.
An FIR should not be quashed if, on its face, it discloses the basic ingredients of a cognizable offense.
The question of whether the alleged offenses can be ultimately proven is a matter for investigation and trial, not for a court to decide at the stage of quashing an FIR.
application: The Supreme Court examined the contents of the FIR to see if the basic ingredients of the alleged offenses were present.
For the offense under Section 506 IPC, the Court noted the FIR contained a "specific averment" that respondent No. 1 threatened the appellant, saying he would "lose his life."
The Court found that this allegation, along with the claims of breaking locks and removing assets, constituted the basic ingredients for the cognizable offenses mentioned in the FIR.
The Court reasoned that the High Court's role was not to determine if the offenses were proven, but only if a case was made out for investigation.
Since the FIR did disclose the necessary ingredients, the Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred in quashing it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, ruling that the High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR. The Court found that the FIR, on its face, clearly disclosed the basic ingredients of the cognizable offenses of house-breaking, theft, and criminal intimidation. It held that determining the truth of these allegations is the responsibility of the investigating agency and the trial court, and it was premature for the High Court to quash the proceedings at the initial stage.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the FIR lodged by the appellant against the respondents under sections 457, 380 and 506 of the IPC.
appellant_arguments: An arbitral award based on a compromise granted the appellant exclusive possession of the shop in question.
A competent court had passed an interim order directing that the assets and belongings of the shop be preserved.
The removal of assets from the shop by the respondents, without the appellant's consent or knowledge and in violation of the court's preservation order, constitutes theft.
respondent_arguments: The allegations in the FIR, even when taken at face value, do not constitute the essential ingredients of the offences under sections 457, 380, and 506 of the IPC.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court cannot quash an FIR if the allegations, taken at face value, prima facie satisfy the ingredients of the alleged offences.
obiter: Observations made by a court when deciding on the quashing of an FIR are only for that specific purpose and must not influence the subsequent investigation or trial, which must be decided independently based on the evidence presented.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR, as the allegations, when considered in light of the factual background, made out a prima facie case for the alleged offences. Specifically, the removal of assets from the shop by the respondents, despite a court order directing that the assets be preserved and an arbitral award granting the appellant exclusive possession, could not be dismissed at the threshold and warranted a full investigation.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the allegations in the First Information Report (FIR), taken at face value, satisfy the essential ingredients of the criminal offences alleged.
policy_considerations: The law should be allowed to take its own course, and criminal proceedings should not be quashed at the initial stage if the allegations disclose a prima facie case that requires investigation.
Observations made by a higher court when deciding whether to quash an FIR should not influence the subsequent investigation or trial, which must proceed independently based on the evidence adduced.
